title: Festive cooking among the Parsis of old Delhi
body: Recalling the Parsis of old Delhi, a writer describes how, at festive gatherings, the women of the community did all the cooking themselves; hiring outside caterers was unheard of. The poorer members of the community never knew who had paid for what. This custom continued in Lucknow, Kanpur and Allahabad well into the 1970s, but that way of life has now almost disappeared. Preparations began two days ahead: dar ni pori, a rich pastry stuffed with sweetened lentils, and malido, a halwa, were carried in big pots and served with puris. The writer says that making malido needs strong biceps; the first time she made it under her grandmother's eye was also the last, and her arms ached for two days. Since then she has had a healthy respect for her dainty grandmother.

title: The Kandur and the breads of Kashmir
body: In Kashmir, the day is said to begin with a cup of hot nun chai, a salty pink tea, and a crisp bread freshly baked by the Kandur, the traditional baker. The Kandur shop is not just a place to buy the morning and evening breads; it is a social hub where people hear and join discussions ranging from gossip to politics. Tsot-Girda is a medium-sized round bread found on every breakfast table. Lavasa is a puffy flat bread made from maida. Tsochwor, a bagel-shaped bread sprinkled with sesame seeds, is baked at noon for afternoon tea. Kulchas are crisp, palm-sized breads, sweet or savoury, eaten with milk kehva. Sheermal is mildly sweet. Roath, a sweet bread with a cake-like texture topped with dry fruits, is made only for grand occasions such as weddings, births and engagements.
